topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: State and prove Cantor's Nested Intervals Theorem.
approach: Define the set of left endpoints, take its supremum $\xi$, and prove $\xi \in [a_n, b_n]$ for all $n$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: I_n = [a_n, b_n], \quad I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N} \implies \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n \ne \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: If $I_n$ is a nested sequence of closed bounded intervals, there exists at least one real number $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$.

solution_steps.title: Properties of Endpoints
solution_steps.math: a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_n \le \dots \le b_m \le \dots \le b_2 \le b_1
solution_steps.explanation: For any $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, $a_n \le a_{\max(n,m)} \le b_{\max(n,m)} \le b_m$. Thus every $b_m$ is an upper bound for $A = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$.

solution_steps.title: Existence of Supremum
solution_steps.math: A = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \ne \emptyset \text{ is bounded above} \implies \xi = \sup A \in \mathbb{R} \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Property of $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Verification that $\xi \in I_n$
solution_steps.math: a_n \le \xi \; (\forall n) \quad \text{and} \quad \xi \le b_n \; (\forall n) \implies a_n \le \xi \le b_n \implies \xi \in [a_n, b_n] = I_n \; (\forall n)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\xi$ is the supremum of $A$, $a_n \le \xi$. Since each $b_n$ is an upper bound for $A$, $\xi \le b_n$. Hence $\xi \in \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n$.

final_answer: $\xi = \sup\{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \in \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n$, so the intersection is non-empty.
exam_tip: If the problem also mentions length tending to zero: $\inf\{b_n - a_n\} = 0 \implies \xi$ is unique.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: State and prove the Monotone Convergence Theorem for bounded sequences.
concept_tested: Monotone Convergence Theorem for Bounded Sequences
approach: State the theorem and prove the increasing case using $x = \sup\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \text{A monotone sequence of real numbers is convergent if and only if it is bounded.}
solution_steps.explanation: Specifically: an increasing sequence bounded above converges to its supremum; a decreasing sequence bounded below converges to its infimum.

solution_steps.title: Setting up the Supremum
solution_steps.math: S = \{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}. \quad S \ne \emptyset \text{ and bounded above} \implies x = \sup S \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Property of $\mathbb{R}$, $x = \sup S$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Applying the $\epsilon$-characterization
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; x - \epsilon < x \implies \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } x_K > x - \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x - \epsilon$ is not an upper bound of $S$.

solution_steps.title: Monotonicity and Conclusion
solution_steps.math: n \ge K \implies x - \epsilon < x_K \le x_n \le x < x + \epsilon \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Because $(x_n)$ is increasing, $x_n \ge x_K$. Since $x$ is an upper bound, $x_n \le x$. Thus $|x_n - x| < \epsilon$ for all $n \ge K$, so $\lim x_n = x$.

final_answer: Every bounded monotone sequence converges. For an increasing sequence, $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = \sup\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$.
exam_tip: Clearly show the two bounds: $x - \epsilon < x_K \le x_n$ (from monotonicity) and $x_n \le x < x + \epsilon$ (from upper bound).

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Let $X = (x_n)$ be a sequence of real numbers that converges to $x$ and $Z = (z_n)$ be a sequence of non-zero real numbers that converges to $z \ne 0$. Prove that $X/Z$ converges to $x/z$.
concept_tested: Quotient Rule for Limits of Sequences
approach: Show that $1/z_n \to 1/z$ using a lower bound for $|z_n|$, then apply the product limit theorem.

solution_steps.title: Bound on $|z_n|$ away from 0
solution_steps.math: \lim z_n = z \ne 0. \quad \text{Set } \epsilon_0 = \frac{|z|}{2} > 0. \quad \exists K_1 : n \ge K_1 \implies |z_n - z| < \frac{|z|}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By reverse triangle inequality, $|z_n| \ge |z| - |z_n - z| > |z| - \frac{|z|}{2} = \frac{|z|}{2}$ for all $n \ge K_1$.

solution_steps.title: Convergence of Reciprocals $1/z_n \to 1/z$
solution_steps.math: \left|\frac{1}{z_n} - \frac{1}{z}\right| = \frac{|z - z_n|}{|z_n||z|} \le \frac{|z_n - z|}{\frac{|z|}{2}|z|} = \frac{2}{|z|^2} |z_n - z|
solution_steps.explanation: Given $\epsilon > 0$, choose $K_2$ such that $n \ge K_2 \implies |z_n - z| < \frac{|z|^2 \epsilon}{2}$. For $n \ge \max(K_1, K_2)$, $|1/z_n - 1/z| < \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Product Limit Law
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{x_n}{z_n} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(x_n \cdot \frac{1}{z_n}\right) = x \cdot \frac{1}{z} = \frac{x}{z}
solution_steps.explanation: Applying the theorem that the limit of a product of convergent sequences is the product of their limits.

exam_tip: The step establishing $|z_n| > |z|/2$ is where most students lose marks if omitted.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded increasing sequence. Prove that $\lim(x_n) = \sup \{x_n \mid n \in \mathbb{N}\}$.
approach: Let $u = \sup\{x_n\}$, use $\epsilon$-definition of supremum, then monotonicity.

solution_steps.title: Existence of Supremum
solution_steps.math: S = \{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}. \quad S \ne \emptyset, \, S \text{ bounded above} \implies u = \sup S \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Axiom of $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Finding Index $K$
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; u - \epsilon < u \implies \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } u - \epsilon < x_K \le u
solution_steps.explanation: Since $u - \epsilon$ is not an upper bound of $S$.

solution_steps.title: Monotonicity Inequality
solution_steps.math: n \ge K \implies u - \epsilon < x_K \le x_n \le u < u + \epsilon \implies |x_n - u| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since $(x_n)$ is increasing, $x_n \ge x_K$. Since $u$ is an upper bound, $x_n \le u$.

exam_tip: State clearly that every term is bounded between $u - \epsilon$ and $u + \epsilon$ for all $n \ge K$.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Show that the sequence of functions $f_n(x) = \frac{x^n}{1+x^n}$ converges pointwise but not uniformly on the interval $[0, 2]$.
approach: Find pointwise limit $f(x)$ on $[0, 2]$, note discontinuity at $x=1$, which rules out uniform convergence.

solution_steps.title: Pointwise Limit Calculation
solution_steps.math: f(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{x^n}{1+x^n} = \begin{cases} 0, & 0 \le x < 1 \\ 1/2, & x = 1 \\ 1, & 1 < x \le 2 \end{cases}

solution_steps.title: Continuity of Individual Functions
solution_steps.math: f_n(x) = \frac{x^n}{1+x^n} \text{ is continuous on } [0, 2] \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $1 + x^n \ge 1 \ne 0$ on $[0, 2]$, $f_n$ is a rational function with non-vanishing denominator, hence continuous.

solution_steps.title: Discontinuity of Limit Function
solution_steps.explanation: $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x = 1$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion on Uniform Convergence
solution_steps.math: (f_n \text{ continuous} \land f_n \rightrightarrows f) \implies f \text{ continuous}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Uniform Limit Theorem, uniform convergence preserves continuity. Since $f$ is discontinuous, $(f_n)$ cannot converge uniformly on $[0, 2]$.

final_answer: $f_n \to f$ pointwise, but NOT uniformly on $[0, 2]$ because the limit function $f$ is discontinuous at $x = 1$.
exam_tip: Using the Uniform Limit Theorem contrapositive is much faster than computing the supremum norm.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Show that every uniformly convergent sequence of bounded functions is uniformly bounded.
concept_tested: Uniform Boundedness of Uniformly Convergent Sequences
approach: Use uniform convergence to bound $|f_n(x) - f(x)| < 1$, then bound $f(x)$, then take maximum over initial functions.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Convergence for $\epsilon = 1$
solution_steps.math: f_n \rightrightarrows f \text{ on } A \implies \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } \forall n \ge H, \; \sup_{x \in A} |f_n(x) - f(x)| < 1
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of uniform convergence with $\epsilon = 1$.

solution_steps.title: Boundedness of Limit Function $f$
solution_steps.math: f_H \text{ is bounded by } M_H \implies |f(x)| \le |f(x) - f_H(x)| + |f_H(x)| < 1 + M_H \; (\forall x \in A)
solution_steps.explanation: Thus the limit function $f$ is bounded on $A$ by $M_f = 1 + M_H$.

solution_steps.title: Bound for $n \ge H$
solution_steps.math: n \ge H \implies |f_n(x)| \le |f_n(x) - f(x)| + |f(x)| < 1 + M_f \; (\forall x \in A)
solution_steps.explanation: All functions beyond index $H$ are uniformly bounded by $1 + M_f$.

solution_steps.title: Global Uniform Bound $M$
solution_steps.math: M = \max\{M_1, M_2, \dots, M_{H-1}, 1 + M_f\} \implies |f_n(x)| \le M \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \; \forall x \in A
solution_steps.explanation: Since each of the first $H-1$ functions is bounded by some $M_k$, taking the maximum over this finite set gives a uniform bound valid for all $n$ and all $x \in A$.

final_answer: There exists $M > 0$ such that $|f_n(x)| \le M$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $x \in A$.
exam_tip: Emphasize that the finite collection $\{f_1, \dots, f_{H-1}\}$ has a maximum bound, which ensures a single global bound $M$.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Let $f_n(x) = \frac{\sin(nx)}{\sqrt{n}}$ for $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Show that $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to 0, but the sequence of derivatives $(f_n')$ does not converge pointwise to 0 on $\mathbb{R}$.
concept_tested: Uniform Convergence vs Differentiation of Sequences

solution_steps.title: Uniform Convergence of $(f_n)$
solution_steps.math: |f_n(x)| = \left|\frac{\sin(nx)}{\sqrt{n}}\right| \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|\sin(u)| \le 1$ for all $u$.

solution_steps.title: Supremum Norm Limit
solution_steps.math: \|f_n - 0\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |f_n(x)| \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \to 0 \text{ as } n \to \infty \implies f_n \rightrightarrows 0 \text{ on } \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to the zero function on $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Compute Derivative $f_n'(x)$
solution_steps.math: f_n'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{\sin(nx)}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = \frac{n\cos(nx)}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{n}\cos(nx)
solution_steps.explanation: By standard differentiation.

solution_steps.title: Evaluate at $x = 0$
solution_steps.math: f_n'(0) = \sqrt{n} \cos(0) = \sqrt{n} \to +\infty \ne 0
solution_steps.explanation: At $x = 0$, $f_n'(0) \to +\infty$, so $(f_n')$ does not converge to $0$ (it diverges).

final_answer: $f_n \rightrightarrows 0$ uniformly, but $f_n'(0) = \sqrt{n} \to \infty$, so $(f_n')$ does not converge pointwise to $(0)' = 0$.
exam_tip: This is the classic example demonstrating why differentiation does not commute with uniform limits without additional conditions on $f_n'$.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Show that every convergent sequence in a metric space is a Cauchy sequence.
concept_tested: Convergent Sequences are Cauchy in Metric Spaces
approach: Use the metric triangle inequality $d(x_n, x_m) \le d(x_n, x) + d(x, x_m)$ with tolerance $\epsilon/2$.

solution_steps.title: Convergence Hypothesis
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x \text{ in } (M, d) \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n \ge H \implies d(x_n, x) < \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of metric convergence.

solution_steps.title: Metric Triangle Inequality
solution_steps.math: d(x_n, x_m) \le d(x_n, x) + d(x, x_m) = d(x_n, x) + d(x_m, x)
solution_steps.explanation: Using triangle inequality and symmetry $d(x, x_m) = d(x_m, x)$.

solution_steps.title: Cauchy Condition
solution_steps.math: n, m \ge H \implies d(x_n, x_m) < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Hence $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $(M, d)$.

final_answer: Every convergent sequence in any metric space is Cauchy.
exam_tip: Always mention the use of both the triangle inequality and symmetry axioms of the metric.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Prove that every convergent sequence of real numbers is a Cauchy sequence.
approach: Apply triangle inequality $|x_n - x_m| \le |x_n - x| + |x_m - x|$ with $\epsilon/2$.

solution_steps.title: Convergence Definition & Setup with $\epsilon/2$
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x \implies \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n \ge H \implies |x_n - x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of sequence convergence, for any chosen tolerance $\epsilon > 0$, the sequence terms eventually lie within $\epsilon/2$ of the limit $x$.

solution_steps.title: Pairing Indices $n, m \ge H$
solution_steps.math: n \ge H \implies |x_n - x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} \quad \text{and} \quad m \ge H \implies |x_m - x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Both indices $n$ and $m$ are greater than or equal to $H$, so both $x_n$ and $x_m$ are within distance $\epsilon/2$ of the target limit $x$.

solution_steps.title: Triangle Inequality & Cauchy Conclusion
solution_steps.math: n, m \ge H \implies |x_n - x_m| = |(x_n - x) + (x - x_m)| \le |x_n - x| + |x_m - x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: By the Triangle Inequality, the distance between any two terms past index $H$ satisfies $|x_n - x_m| < \epsilon$. Therefore, $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence.

final_answer: Every convergent sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
exam_tip: State that the converse also holds in $\mathbb{R}$ (Cauchy Convergence Criterion / Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$).

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: State and prove the Monotone Convergence Theorem for sequences.
approach: Prove both directions: bounded monotone implies convergent; convergent implies bounded.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \text{A monotone sequence of real numbers is convergent } \iff \text{it is bounded.}
solution_steps.explanation: Convergence implies boundedness (for all sequences). For monotone sequences, boundedness also implies convergence.

solution_steps.title: Convergence $\implies$ Boundedness
solution_steps.math: x_n \to x \implies (x_n) \text{ is bounded}
solution_steps.explanation: Every convergent sequence is bounded (choose $\epsilon=1$, $M = \max\{|x_1|, \dots, |x_{K-1}|, |x|+1\}$).

solution_steps.title: Boundedness $\implies$ Convergence (Increasing case)
solution_steps.math: x_n \le x_{n+1}, \, x_n \le M \implies u = \sup\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, the supremum $u$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Verification of Limit
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K : u - \epsilon < x_K \le x_n \le u < u + \epsilon \; (\forall n \ge K) \implies \lim x_n = u
solution_steps.explanation: This shows $x_n \to u$.

final_answer: A monotone sequence converges if and only if it is bounded. If $(x_n)$ is increasing and bounded, $\lim x_n = \sup\{x_n\}$; if decreasing and bounded, $\lim x_n = \inf\{x_n\}$.
exam_tip: Remember to address the $(\implies)$ direction as well since the theorem is an 'if and only if' statement.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Prove that a sequence of real numbers is convergent if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.
approach: Prove both: $(\implies)$ convergent is Cauchy; $(\impliedby)$ Cauchy is bounded, has convergent subsequence by Bolzano-Weierstrass, then converges to same limit.

solution_steps.title: Direction 1 ($\implies$): Convergent $\implies$ Cauchy
solution_steps.math: |x_n - x_m| \le |x_n - x| + |x_m - x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon \quad (n, m \ge H)
solution_steps.explanation: Proved using the triangle inequality.

solution_steps.title: Direction 2 ($\impliedby$): Step 2a — Cauchy is Bounded
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \text{ is Cauchy} \implies (x_n) \text{ is bounded}
solution_steps.explanation: Fix $\epsilon = 1$, all terms beyond $H$ lie in $(x_H - 1, x_H + 1)$.

solution_steps.title: Step 2b — Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \text{ bounded} \implies \exists \text{ subsequence } (x_{n_k}) \text{ converging to some } x^* \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ contains a convergent subsequence.

solution_steps.title: Step 2c — Parent Sequence Converges to $x^*$
solution_steps.math: |x_n - x^*| \le |x_n - x_{n_k}| + |x_{n_k} - x^*| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon \quad \text{for large } n, k
solution_steps.explanation: Since $n_k \ge k \ge H$ and $n \ge H$, the Cauchy property traps $x_n$ close to $x_{n_k}$, which is close to $x^*$.

final_answer: A sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ converges if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.
exam_tip: The chain of logic for completeness: Cauchy $\implies$ bounded $\implies$ Bolzano-Weierstrass gives convergent subsequence $\implies$ entire Cauchy sequence converges.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Show that the sequence $(x_n)$ defined by $x_1 = 1$ and $x_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + x_n}$ is convergent and find its limit.
approach: Use mathematical induction to show bounded and increasing, apply Monotone Convergence Theorem, then solve the algebraic limit equation.

solution_steps.title: Induction: Bounded above by 2
solution_steps.math: x_1 = 1 < 2. \quad \text{Assume } x_k < 2 \implies x_{k+1} = \sqrt{2 + x_k} < \sqrt{2 + 2} = 2
solution_steps.explanation: By induction, $x_n < 2$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

solution_steps.title: Induction: Monotonically Increasing
solution_steps.math: x_1 = 1 < x_2 = \sqrt{3}. \quad x_k < x_{k+1} \implies 2 + x_k < 2 + x_{k+1} \implies \sqrt{2 + x_k} < \sqrt{2 + x_{k+1}} \implies x_{k+1} < x_{k+2}
solution_steps.explanation: By induction, $x_n < x_{n+1}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

solution_steps.title: Monotone Convergence Theorem
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \text{ is increasing and bounded above} \implies L = \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: The limit $L$ exists and $L > 0$ since $x_n \ge 1$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate Limit
solution_steps.math: L = \sqrt{2 + L} \implies L^2 = 2 + L \implies L^2 - L - 2 = 0 \implies (L - 2)(L + 1) = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x_n > 0$, $L \ge 1 > 0$, discarding $L = -1$ gives $L = 2$.

exam_tip: You must prove convergence BEFORE writing $L = \sqrt{2+L}$; writing the equation first assumes the limit exists.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Let $X = (x_n)$ be a sequence of real numbers and let $m \in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that the $m$-tail $X_m = (x_{n+m})$ of $X$ converges if and only if $X$ converges, and $\lim X = \lim X_m$.
approach: Use the definition of limit and index shift $k = n + m$.

solution_steps.title: Definition of $m$-tail
solution_steps.explanation: The sequence obtained by discarding the first $m$ terms.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction: $X \to x \implies X_m \to x$
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists K : n \ge K \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon. \quad \text{For } X_m, \text{ if } n \ge K, \text{ then } n + m > n \ge K \implies |x_{n+m} - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: So $X_m$ converges to $x$ (with cutoff index $K_m = \max(1, K - m)$).

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction: $X_m \to x \implies X \to x$
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists K_m : n \ge K_m \implies |x_{n+m} - x| < \epsilon. \quad \text{Set } K = K_m + m. \text{ For } p \ge K, p - m \ge K_m \implies |x_p - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $X$ converges to $x$.

final_answer: The $m$-tail $X_m$ converges if and only if $X$ converges, and $\lim X_m = \lim X$.
exam_tip: This theorem formally justifies why finitely many initial terms never affect convergence or the value of the limit.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Construct a sequence $(s_n)$ of real numbers that converges to $\sqrt{5}$ and is correct to within 4 decimal places.
concept_tested: Construction of Sequence Converging to $\sqrt{5}$ (Newton's Method)

solution_steps.title: Recurrence Formula
solution_steps.math: s_1 = 2, \quad s_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2} \left(s_n + \frac{5}{s_n}\right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 1
solution_steps.explanation: Newton-Raphson iteration for solving $f(x) = x^2 - 5 = 0$.

solution_steps.title: Computing Iterates
solution_steps.explanation: First iteration.

solution_steps.title: Second and Third Iterates
solution_steps.math: s_3 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{9}{4} + \frac{20}{9}\right) = \frac{161}{72} \approx 2.236111\dots, \quad s_4 = \frac{1}{2}\left(s_3 + \frac{5}{s_3}\right) \approx 2.236067977
solution_steps.explanation: Evaluating successive terms.

solution_steps.title: Error Bound
solution_steps.explanation: $s_3 = 161/72$ is already accurate to 4 decimal places ($2.2361$). $s_4$ is accurate to 8 decimal places.

final_answer: The sequence is defined by $s_1 = 2, s_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}(s_n + 5/s_n)$. The term $s_3 = \frac{161}{72} \approx 2.2361$ approximates $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236068$ correct to 4 decimal places.
exam_tip: Show the fraction $161/72$ and its decimal value to prove accuracy within $0.0001$.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: State and prove the Monotone Subsequence Theorem.
approach: Define peak points: $x_m$ is a peak if $x_m \ge x_n$ for all $n > m$. Case 1: infinitely many peaks; Case 2: finitely many peaks.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \text{Every sequence of real numbers } (x_n) \text{ has a monotonic subsequence.}
solution_steps.explanation: Either a monotonically increasing or monotonically decreasing subsequence always exists.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Peak
solution_steps.math: x_m \text{ is a peak if } x_m \ge x_n \quad \forall n > m
solution_steps.explanation: A term is a peak if no subsequent term strictly exceeds it.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: Infinitely Many Peaks
solution_steps.math: m_1 < m_2 < m_3 < \dots \text{ (peak indices)} \implies x_{m_1} \ge x_{m_2} \ge x_{m_3} \ge \dots
solution_steps.explanation: The subsequence of peaks $(x_{m_k})$ is a decreasing sequence.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: Finitely Many Peaks (or No Peaks)
solution_steps.math: s_1 > \text{last peak} \implies \exists s_2 > s_1 \text{ s.t. } x_{s_2} > x_{s_1}; \quad \exists s_3 > s_2 \text{ s.t. } x_{s_3} > x_{s_2}, \dots
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x_{s_1}$ is not a peak, there exists $s_2 > s_1$ with $x_{s_2} > x_{s_1}$. Continuing inductively produces a strictly increasing subsequence $x_{s_1} < x_{s_2} < x_{s_3} < \dots$.

final_answer: Every sequence has a monotonic subsequence (decreasing if infinitely many peaks, increasing if finitely many peaks).
exam_tip: This theorem is the fastest and most elegant way to prove the Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Let $x_1 = 2$ and $x_{n+1} = 2 + \frac{1}{x_n}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Show that $(x_n)$ is a contractive sequence, and find its limit.
concept_tested: Contractive Sequences and Fixed Point Limits
approach: Show $|x_{n+2} - x_{n+1}| \le C |x_{n+1} - x_n|$ with $C < 1$, then solve $L = 2 + 1/L$.

solution_steps.title: Terms and Bounds
solution_steps.math: x_1 = 2, \quad x_2 = 2 + 1/2 = 2.5, \quad x_n \ge 2 \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x_1 = 2$ and $x_{n+1} = 2 + 1/x_n > 2$ by induction.

solution_steps.title: Contractive Verification
solution_steps.math: |x_{n+2} - x_{n+1}| = \left|\left(2 + \frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right) - \left(2 + \frac{1}{x_n}\right)\right| = \frac{|x_n - x_{n+1}|}{x_n x_{n+1}}
solution_steps.explanation: Compute the difference between successive terms.

solution_steps.title: Contractive Constant $C$
solution_steps.math: x_n \ge 2, \, x_{n+1} \ge 2 \implies x_n x_{n+1} \ge 4 \implies |x_{n+2} - x_{n+1}| \le \frac{1}{4} |x_{n+1} - x_n|
solution_steps.explanation: Since $C = 1/4 < 1$, the sequence is contractive.

solution_steps.title: Convergence and Limit
solution_steps.math: L = 2 + \frac{1}{L} \implies L^2 - 2L - 1 = 0 \implies L = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 4}}{2} = 1 \pm \sqrt{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x_n \ge 2 > 0$, $L > 0$, so $L = 1 + \sqrt{2}$.

final_answer: $(x_n)$ is contractive with constant $C = 1/4 < 1$, hence it converges to $L = 1 + \sqrt{2}$.
exam_tip: Note that every contractive sequence is Cauchy, and hence convergent in $\mathbb{R}$.
